reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it teaches viewers to purchase OneCoin from a trading balance, including a ten-coin minimum, a euro price, and entry of a transaction password. It reinforces the solicitation with claims about automatic token purchases, processing fees, future coin credits, and earning OneCoins, while advising viewers to assume an order succeeded without browser confirmation. The speaker does not execute the order on screen, and the available video evidence does not establish an actual charge, deposit, or realized return.

citations.quote: use the trading account to purchase ONE coin
they will purchase tokens on your behalf which then get automatically submitted to earn OneCoins for you
you're gonna see the transaction value and you're gonna put in your transaction password

opening.argument: The account process is described with contingencies rather than a guaranteed investment outcome: the speaker says it is possible that token availability may be insufficient and presents company purchasing as a fallback. That language leaves room for uncertainty and does not promise appreciation, profit, or a guaranteed return. The speaker also characterizes the activity as a personal account routine, saying they already completed it and would not submit another order. The strongest reading is a walkthrough of conditional mechanics, not an assurance that viewers will make money.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference emphasizes the password field, processing fee, and future credits, but those points identify steps and stated account behavior, not proof of deception or a guaranteed financial result. The speaker even warns about missing browser confirmation and instructs the viewer to place the order only once, which is operational guidance about avoiding duplication. The cited evidence does not establish that the speaker promises profit or claims the transaction is risk-free.

citations.quote: Sometimes in certain browsers you do not get a window that pops up
Keep that in mind and place the order one time

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Conditional wording does not function as a meaningful risk warning when the same explanation tells viewers that purchased coins will appear and that tokens will be submitted to earn OneCoins. The audience is reassured not to worry if the credits are absent, while the purchase process and password entry are made actionable. Uncertainty about timing or availability is not the same as disclosing that the promised earning mechanism may be unreliable.

opening.argument: This is most naturally understood as an operational tutorial. The title explicitly presents the subject as how to buy OneCoin from an account, and the narration walks through opening the exchange, selecting ONE, entering the quantity and transaction password, and placing the order. The speaker distinguishes the trading-account procedure from the cash-account procedure and explains how the payment method changes. That instructional structure supports an education or demonstration classification, regardless of whether a viewer ultimately chooses to use the service.

These are the same exact steps, except that when you use the payment method

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the video a tutorial does not itself show that it is a scam. The speaker describes a procedure and says the order was already completed earlier, rather than presenting a completed on-screen purchase as proof of success. The reference's focus on the interface and workflow is therefore consistent with a technology or account-operation demonstration, and it does not establish that viewers were deceived.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A tutorial can still be promotional scam content when it gives viewers concrete instructions to buy and links that purchase to earning additional coins. Here, the walkthrough does more than describe software: it directs the viewer through quantity, payment method, password, and order placement, then explains what the purchased tokens supposedly do. Its instructional format makes the solicitation actionable rather than neutral.

opening.argument: The visible material can be read as ordinary account commerce: an exchange-style buy form offers a market order, displays a current euro price, identifies payment-account choices, and provides a place-order control. The frames show an order interface and account balances, but they do not establish that an order was successfully completed, that money was actually charged, that coins were delivered, or that any return was realized. A purchase interface and instructions for using it are not by themselves proof of a scam mechanism.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference treats the displayed password field, price, and account balances as evidence of solicitation, but those are ordinary components of an online purchase workflow. Its own position acknowledges that the order was not executed on screen and that no charge, deposit, or realized return is established. The available evidence therefore supports an account-use demonstration without proving the alleged scam mechanism.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a completed charge does not remove the solicitation: the video instructs viewers to use account balances to purchase coins and explains that the purchased tokens will be submitted to earn more OneCoins. The interface is not merely a generic retail checkout; it is tied to a token-purchase-and-earning pathway, with the speaker telling viewers what to enter and how to respond when confirmation is missing.
